extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, appellate attorneys, judges, and patent practitioners involved in §101 eligibility disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria for evaluating whether patent claims are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101 using the two-step Alice framework, and related procedural standards for dismissal and leave to amend on §101 grounds. Geared to assessing claims and pleadings in litigation and on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility is evaluated under Alice: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (an 'abstract idea'); and (2) if so, determine whether the claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, provide an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply step 1 to identify the focus of the claims; if the claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea, proceed to step 2 to ask whether the claim contains something 'more' than the abstract idea—an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed-to-abstract-idea criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea if they focus on collecting, analyzing, and/or displaying information or otherwise recite only the result or desired outcome without describing how to achieve it technologically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court will characterize the claims' focus; overly broad characterizations (e.g., merely 'collecting geographic information and displaying nearby stores') support finding an abstract idea when the claims lack technological detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for technological details or improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid abstraction, claims must recite a particular assertedly inventive technology or improvement in computer functionality rather than generic functional language describing desired results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that 'merely use functional language to describe the desired result, without any technological details about how that result is implemented or that improves on existing computer technology' are susceptible to §101 invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting/analyzing/displaying information is ordinarily abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are limited to gathering, analyzing, and displaying information—even if directed to a particular field—are generally treated as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Electric Power Group: tracking real-time changes and displaying results without claiming a particular way of collecting/analyzing/displaying is abstract. Limitations that only organize existing information into a new form do not overcome abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete, specific rule-based implementations can be eligible (McRO example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite detailed, specific computerized rules or relationships that materially change how a task is performed can be patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McRO upheld claims because they required rules rendered in a specific way (relationships between sub-sequences of phonemes, timing, and morph weight sets) and thus went beyond merely organizing information or automating conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement at Alice step 2
rubrics_metrics.description: At step 2, claims must include an inventive concept beyond well-understood, routine, conventional computer components or techniques; generic implementation on a computer is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry asks whether limitations are described in highly generic functional terms and whether the patent 'invoke[s] any assertedly inventive programming,' 'new technique[s] for analyzing' data, or 'an arguably inventive set of components or methods' that generate new data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection/organization of information is an ordinary mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting information by content or source for collection, analysis, and display is treated as an ordinary mental process and does not, by itself, confer an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely selecting a brand via an icon versus typing its name (a user-interface convenience) is an example of something arising from conventional computer technology rather than an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting to a field of endeavor does not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Restricting an abstract idea to a particular field (e.g., mapping or locating businesses) generally does not make the claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electric Power Group and similar precedents hold that field-specific limits do not transform a claim directed to information processing into patent-eligible subject matter absent a technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed/efficiency improvements via conventional computers are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming that added computer functionality increases the speed or efficiency of a process does not render an otherwise abstract idea patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One: 'merely adding computer functionality to increase the speed or efficiency of the process does not confer patent eligibility on an otherwise abstract idea.'

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as an 'inventive' technical contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventive contribution may be a new source or type of information, a new technique for analyzing it, an inventive combination of components/methods that generate new data, or non-routine programming—rather than routine use of conventional components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims lacking any of these (i.e., relying on conventional GPS, touchscreens, off-the-shelf components) typically fail step 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification admissions on conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in the patent specification admitting that components or techniques are conventional (e.g., that devices have GPS, display maps, search for businesses) can establish that claim limitations are well-known and routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification that acknowledges that generic and pre-existing computer functionality can perform all claimed steps limits plausible allegations that components were unconventional and thus can support §101 dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal standard on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: On a 12(b)(6) motion, courts assume all well-pleaded allegations are true and draw all reasonable inferences in the plaintiff's favor; the Seventh Circuit reviews such dismissals de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing a district court's 12(b)(6) dismissal, appellate courts evaluate whether the complaint states a plausible claim for relief under the applicable legal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of leave to amend for futility
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court's denial of leave to amend is reviewed for abuse of discretion, but if denial is based on futility the court applies the legal sufficiency standard of Rule 12(b)(6) (i.e., de novo review of whether an amended complaint would state a claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave may be denied when any amendment would be futile—e.g., where the patent specification and intrinsic record demonstrate as a matter of law that the claims are directed to ineligible subject matter and cannot be cured by additional allegations or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Circuit review of §101 issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit reviews the ultimate determination of patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While district courts make the initial eligibility determination (and factual matters may be relevant), the Federal Circuit applies its own law in reviewing §101 questions on appeal.
